extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in disinformation and online influence
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-style overview describing what internet manipulation is, its aims and techniques, psychological and algorithmic mechanisms that make it effective, documented examples (state and non-state), countermeasures, and national regulatory responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of internet manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet manipulation is the use of online digital technologies, including algorithms, social bots, and automated scripts, for commercial, social, military, or political purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes computational propaganda as internet manipulation for propaganda purposes and links the concept to disinformation spread on digital platforms used for media consumption and everyday communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes and intended effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When employed for political purposes, internet manipulation may be used to steer public opinion, polarise citizens, circulate conspiracy theories, and silence political dissidents; it can also be used for profit to harm adversaries or improve brand reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also includes selective enforcement of Internet censorship or violations of net neutrality as forms of manipulation; the harms range from economic damage to erosion of individual autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic personalization and exposure restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms tailor and personalize users' feeds based on preferences, which can restrict exposure to different viewpoints and lead to echo chambers or filter bubbles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms give the impression that a particular point of view is widely shared and may amplify polarization even if they are not sole causes; personalization diminishes pluralism and range of choice in information exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological levers that increase virality
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that evokes high-arousal emotions (awe, anger, anxiety, sexual meaning) or that is surprising, interesting, or useful tends to be more viral; simple explanations for complex issues are easier to believe and spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines and sound bites alone can have effects without being read in full; research (e.g., Berger & Milkman) supports emotional arousal and novelty as drivers of sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social proof and prior ratings influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior collective ratings or early votes influence others' perceptions and subsequent evaluations (bandwagon/snowball voting), affecting whether content gains or loses popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments and platform observations (e.g., Reddit vote dynamics, manipulated confederate ratings in art evaluation) show early signals shape downstream engagement; hiding vote counts is a mitigation used by some sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of an information operations campaign (Facebook report)
rubrics_metrics.description: An information operations campaign commonly involves three components: targeted data collection, content creation, and false amplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of these components include stealing and exposing non-public information; spreading stories (false or real) via fake accounts; and coordinating fake accounts to amplify certain voices while repressing others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific covert tactics (JTRIG/GCHQ example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics include injecting false material, posting material falsely attributed to others, pretending to be victims of targets, posting negative information to destroy reputation, mass messaging/pushing stories, false-flag operations, changing photographs, credential harvesting, and using journalists to disseminate manipulated material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described in leaked documents about GCHQ's Joint Threat Research Intelligence Group (JTRIG); characterized as 'dirty tricks' and 'effects' operations aimed to 'destroy, deny, degrade [and] disrupt' targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated accounts and bot typology
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet bots such as social bots, votebots, and clickbots are software tools used to manipulate online metrics, spread content, and influence perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bots have been used for automated voting, fake likes, click fraud, and amplifying narratives; typologies (e.g., Gorwa & Guilbeault) inform research and policy responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trolling, hacktivism and coordinated human-driven manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hackers, hired professionals, and private citizens engage in internet manipulation through trolling, coordinated campaigns, ballot stuffing, and other crowd actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 4chan's manipulation of an online Time poll and organized 'political trolls' employed by parties; human-driven campaigns may combine technical tools with social engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors that make corrections ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarifications, conspiracy-busting, and fact-checks often come late and may not reach the majority of the audience exposed to the misinformation, limiting their remedial effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because false claims can spread rapidly via headlines and emotional content, corrective information may arrive after harm is done or fail to achieve equal reach or salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychometric targeting and microtargeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of social media and other data can be used to infer personality traits and predict behavior and preferences, enabling tailored persuasive content aimed at individuals' psyches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work by researchers (e.g., Michal Kosinski) and reports about targeted advertising suggest psychographic profiling can be used in political persuasion (noted in discussions of the 2016 U.S. election).

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-level countermeasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform responses include hiding vote counts for a time, flagging posts as likely satire or false, identifying and suspending fake accounts, and collaborating with outside fact-checkers to mark disputed articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Reddit hid vote counts temporarily; Facebook announced disputed articles would be marked and suspended accounts ahead of elections; platforms seek technical ways to detect information operations and fake accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance, openness, and community moderation as defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness and community governance (e.g., Wikipedia's volunteer editors and governance systems) are proposed as ways to surface truth without concentrating power to decide truth in a few companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tim Berners-Lee argues that distributed governance and editorial communities can help determine truth; this is presented as an alternative to centralized content adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical tools for countering misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Software solutions may include fact-checking tools, voluntary browser extensions that record visited sites, or tools using browsing history to present corrective information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes such software exists but flags some claims as possible original research; technical tools are one part of broader mitigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and media literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach formal logic, critical analytic thinking, media literacy, and objective evaluation to help individuals resist manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (e.g., Daniel Suarez) call for education reforms to build critical thinking skills; media literacy is presented as a long-term societal defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approach — Germany (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political actors in Germany publicly committed not to use social bots during an election period; some German states proposed laws that would criminalize violating platform terms (e.g., using pseudonyms or creating fake accounts) with potential imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures combine voluntary party commitments and potential legal penalties; presented as national-level responses to bot use and manipulation before elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approach — Italy (AGCOM guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italy's Communications Agency (AGCOM) published guidelines targeting elections with six main topics: Political Subjects' Equal Treatment; Political Propaganda's Transparency; Contents Illicit and Activities Whose Dissemination Is Forbidden (e.g., Polls); Social Media Accounts of Public Administrations; Political Propaganda Forbidden on Election Day and Day Before; Recommendations for stronger fact-checking services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AGCOM's guidelines are procedural topics meant to frame platform and campaign conduct around elections and to encourage stronger fact-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approach — France (law details and criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: France passed a law (Nov 2018) stipulating that during campaign periods digital platforms must disclose amount paid for ads and names of their authors, have a representative present in France past certain traffic thresholds, and publish the algorithms used; an interim judge may halt the spread of 'fake news' if it is (a) manifest, (b) disseminated on a massive scale, and (c) leads to disturbance of the peace or compromises the outcome of an election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law couples platform transparency requirements with an emergency injunctive remedy against large-scale, manifest falsehoods that threaten public order or electoral outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approach — Malaysia (Anti-Fake News Act example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Malaysia's Anti-Fake News Act defined fake news as 'news, information, data and reports which is or are wholly or partly false' and made violations punishable by imprisonment (the law was later repealed after criticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of a broad criminalization approach that faced political and public backlash; highlights trade-offs and risks of overbroad laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approach — Kenya (Computer and Cybercrimes bill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kenya criminalized intentionally publishing false, misleading or fictitious data or misinforming with intent that the data be considered authentic, subject to fines and up to two years imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another example of criminalization focused on intent to cause data to be treated as authentic; details differ by jurisdiction and raise enforcement and free-speech considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical research findings and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Research indicates mixed findings: some studies suggest social media and search engines increase ideological distance and echo chambers, while reviews show empirical evidence does not fully support the most pessimistic views about polarization; individual choices also drive filtering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites multiple studies (e.g., Flaxman, Goel & Rao; Pariser; Flaxman et al.) showing nuance: algorithms can amplify polarization but may not be the sole cause; evidence is complex and evolving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical harms and timing of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars argue that internet manipulation can harm individuals economically and, more insidiously, challenge individual autonomy; effects are often not apparent until after the harm has been done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion emphasizes the latent, cumulative, and often delayed nature of harms from manipulation, informing why preventive and systemic responses are recommended.
